power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: BFI LLM Prediction Study - Summer 2026
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Our study seeks to address the question, can large-language models (LLMs) such as Anthropic's Claude predict people's Big Five Inventory (BFI) personality profiles from a brief (~ 500 word) text-based interaction with an LLM? We predict that there will be positive, statistically significant correlations between the personality traits generated by Claude and participants' actual Big Five Inventory (BFI) scores for each big  five trait: extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness, and agreeableness.
table.design_dependent_variables: The dependent variable is the Pearson correlation coefficients between Claude's predicted Big Five trait scores and participants' self-reported scores.
table.study_design_overview: This correlational study has a single condition. Participants will complete the 44-item version of the Big Five Inventory (John, Donahue & Kentle, 1991). They will then have an unstructured, text-based interaction with GPT 4.1 requiring 26 turns. Participants will be instructed to get to know the AI, interacting with it as they would a new friend. Following the interaction, participants will complete a post chat Questionnaire (Castiello et al., 2026) to assess the extent to which they connected with the AI.
table.statistical_tests:
Participant's trait scores from their completed BFI-44 questionnaire, as well as the transcript from their text-based LLM interaction will be collected for analyses. Their transcripts will be given to Claude Sonnet 4.6. Claude will be prompted to assess each participant's personality profile, focusing solely on what the participant said during the interaction (i.e. vocabulary choices, topics discussed, emotional tones and interpersonal styles). Claude will then be asked to complete the BFI-44 questionnaire as if it were the participant. Mean scores for each of the five BFI traits will be subsequently calculated from Claude's responses.

We will conduct a correlation analysis between Claude's predicted scores and participants' self-reported scores for each of the five BFI-44 traits. We will control for multiple comparisons by applying a Holm-Bonferroni correction. Statistical significance will be assessed using corrected p-values at an alpha level of 0.05. We will also calculate the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between the predicted and actual scores for each trait.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants who fail the attention checks in our study's questionnaires, as well as those who do not complete the entirety of the study (both the questionnaires and the AI chatbot interaction), will be excluded from further analyses. Participants who write fewer than 130 words (less than 5 words per turn) in their interaction with the LLM will be excluded from further analyses.
table.sample_size: We will collect data from 100 participants via Prolific. Participants will be native English speakers recruited from the UK, the US, and Canada. The sample size is based on a pilot study where we observed statistically significant correlations between self-report BFI scores, and LLM (Claude)-predicted BFI scores, with 50 people.
table.additional_comments:
We predict that the strength of the correlations between LLM-predicted and actual BFI trait scores will depend on the number of messages from each participant that Claude is given. As the number of participant messages used in the prediction decreases from 26 messages to 13 to 5, the average correlation across each of the five BFI traits will decrease. 

The prompt used by Claude to predict BFI scores is posted here: https://github.com/drlametti/bfi_prediction_study

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 192 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified

21 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

In a preregistered study, 100 participants completed the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI) and then engaged in unstructured, text-based conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.

In Castiello et al. (2026) https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/redj/?noauthor=1 100 participants completed the BFI and then had conversations with two versions of GPT-4.1-one instructed to mirror their personality through language, and the other instructed to present the inverse (or opposite) of their personality.
We recruited 200 participants from Prolific-100 for Experiment 1 and 100 for Experiment 2.
Participants were native English speakers aged 18 to 50 from Canada, the US, and the UK.
Participants were excluded if they failed to complete the study, failed an attention check embedded in the questionnaire, or wrote fewer than 130 words during the LLM interaction.
Participants were compensated for their time at £10/hour (Experiment 1) and £7/hour (Experiment 2).
Participants completed the experiment on their own computer.
Participants completed the 44-item version of the Big Five Inventory (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/AwJp/?prefix=BFI%3B John et al., 2012).
Participants had unstructured, text-based conversations with GPT-4.1 (OpenAI) instructed to mimic a specific BFI trait profile through language.
Following completion of the consent form, participants completed the BFI-44 (John et al., 2012).
Participants were blind to the length of the interaction.
Ninety-nine participants completed the BFI questionnaire, and then had an unstructured chat with the LLM GPT-4.1.
Using a similar method to Experiment 1, 95 participants completed the BFI, and then had an unstructured chat with two LLMs.
Participants had conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.

For example, Lucas et al., (2014) demonstrated that participants were willing to disclose more personal information to a virtual human when they believed it was being controlled by a computer versus a person.

info.title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI

author.affiliation:
Department of Experimental Psychology
								University of Oxford

text.text: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits.
Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI).
In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.
We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats.
Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members.
A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater's predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax.
Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI's persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation.
A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1-one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI).
The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report.
Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone.
People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI's persona mirrors the users.
Every week, more than a billion people have conversations with AI systems like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
Here we investigate the extent to which the words we choose to use in human-AI interactions convey our personality traits.

We show that personality traits can be predicted from only a few hundred words of unstructured conversation with AI, and this is enhanced if the AI's persona mirrors the person's personality-a phenomenon that may occur in both human-to-human and human-AI interactions.
The findings imply that people are sharing a great deal of their psychological profile with technology companies in even short interactions with language-based AI systems.
More than a billion people talk with large language models (LLMs) every week (OpenAI, 2026).

text.text: How much information do we convey about our personality in conversations with AI?
And to what extent does the persona of the AI shape what we transmit?

Here, in a preregistered experiment and a second study involving the reanalysis of published data, we address these questions by testing whether Big Five personality traits can be predicted from short, unstructured chats with AI.
The Big Five model is a trait taxonomy of human personality with five dimensions-openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (OCEAN).

The model has its roots in the lexical hypothesis of human personality-or the idea that the important psychological traits that differentiate people are reflected in natural language (e.g., Dan is studious, while Robin is lazy) (Galton, 1884; John et al., 1988).

text.text: How much of our personality do we convey in short conversations?
And, if personality seeps into these interactions, does the fidelity of the signal depend on the personality of our conversational partners?
Here, we address these questions using LLMs, which people increasingly have conversations with.

In a preregistered study, 100 participants completed the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI) and then engaged in unstructured, text-based conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.
GPT-4.1 was instructed to act like a friend during the conversation, and to convey an average Big Five personality profile through language.
A second LLM rater-Claude Sonnet 4.6-was then tasked with predicting each participant's Big Five profile based on the text of the conversation alone.
We hypothesized that correlations between the rater's predicted traits scores and participants' self-reported scores, would be positive and significant for all Big Five traits.
We also predicted that the strength of these correlations would depend on the proportion of the conversation the rater was given.
In a second experiment, we used data we collected previously to replicate and extend the results of Experiment 1.
Both humans and LLMs come to mirror the word choice of conversational partners (Blevins, 2026; P. Chen et al., 2026; Garrod & Anderson, 1987).

text.text: In the present study, we had the LLM rater predict participants' personality traits based on the text of these conversations.
These predictions were then correlated with participants' self-reported traits, and the correlations were compared between mirror and inverse AI chats.

We hypothesized that correlations between the LLM rater's predicted traits scores and participants' self-reported trait scores, would be stronger when the rater's predictions were based on conversations with an LLM that mirrored personality.
Finally, in both experiments we tested the extent to which the LLM rater used lexical information, as opposed to syntax and conversational context, to predict personality traits.

If personality is conveyed largely through the words people use, the LLM rater should be able to reliably predict participants' personality using only a list of content words and pronouns shared by participants in each conversation.

The LLM started each conversation with, Hey, how are you?

text.text: The LLM rater inferred answers to the BFI-44 10 times for each participant in independent runs.

As there was some variability in the inference from run to run (the average SD across traits was .14 of a point on the 1 to 5 scale), we computed BFI trait scores for each of the 10 runs and then we found the average BFI trait scores across the runs.

The primary preregistered hypothesis (Experiment 1) was that, based on text from an unstructured 26-turn interaction with an LLM, the rater could predict participants' BFI traits at greater than chance.
To test this, we computed two-tailed Pearson correlations for each trait between the rater's inferred trait scores and participants' actual self-reported scores.

Permutation tests-in which the correlation was computed 10,000 times based on a random pairing of predicted trait scores with actual trait scores-identified whether the target or experimentally observed Pearson correlation fell outside the permuted null distribution.

As a secondary preregistered hypothesis (Experiment 1), we predicted that the rater's ability to infer participants' BFI traits would decrease if the rater was given fewer than the total number of 26 conversational turns from each chat.
To test this, we chose a random sample of 13 turns for each participant.
Based on this fixed selection, the LLM rater inferred answers to the BFI-44 10 times for each participant in independent runs.
Trait scores were found for each run, and then averaged across the 10 runs.
We then selected 5 random turns from the selection of 13 turns (that is, the 5 turns were nested within the 13), and the rater repeated the inference.
We computed correlations for each trait between the rater-predicted trait scores with 13 and 5 conversational turns and participants' actual self-reported scores.
We also examined the extent to which the LLM rater's predictions of personality traits depended on conversational context and syntax versus lexical content alone.
To do this, the rater generated predictions based on the text participants wrote without the conversational LLM's responses.
We also had the rater generate predictions based solely on the nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs that each participant wrote.

These words were presented to the rater in syntactic categories with the words arranged in alphabetical order (e.g., nouns: baseball, house, river; pronouns: I, them; verbs: hit, run, swam; adjectives: blue, smooth; adverbs: normally, quite).
Correlations were then used to compare these predictions to participants' actual self-reported scores.
For both the turn and lexical analyses, we calculated the mean squared error (MSE) as a measure of overall discrepancy between the LLM-predicted and self-reported scores.
Specifically, for each participant and trait, we calculated the squared difference between predicted and self-reported trait scores.
We then averaged squared errors across traits to generate a single measure of error for each participant, i.e., MSE.
This error was then compared across conditions using one-way repeated measures ANOVA.

In Experiment 2, we compared correlations generated from the same individuals-specifically, correlations between self-reported personality and the rater's predicted personality based on chats with the mirror AI or the inverse AI.
This analysis used Williams' test for dependent correlations (Steiger, 1980).

text.text: As in Experiment 1, we used repeated measures ANOVA to compare MSE between conditions and traits.
We used two-tailed Pearson correlations and a Type I error (α) level of .05, adjusting this threshold for multiple comparisons using a Holm-Bonferroni correction.
Average correlations across traits were calculated using Fisher z-transformation.
Correlations are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Experiment 1 tested the extent to which personality traits are conveyed in brief text-based interactions with AI.
Ninety-nine participants completed the BFI questionnaire, and then had an unstructured chat with the LLM GPT-4.1.
These interactions were 26 conversational turns, with participants writing a median of 430 words (range: 134 to 1431).
A second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) identified elements in their text that revealed information about their personality.
The rater then completed the BFI acting like each participant, mimicking their selections based on its analysis.

text.text: The highest correlation was observed for Neuroticism (r(97) = .47, 95% CI [.29, .60], p < .001) and the lowest for Conscientiousness (r(97) = .25, 95% CI [.05, .42], p = .013; see Appendix 2).

text.text: In two cases-Neuroticism and Agreeableness-the correlations were numerically greater than meta-analytic self-other correlations from family.
Taken together, this provides evidence for our primary preregistered hypothesis: meaningful personality signals emerge in short, unscripted interactions with LLMs.
In a second preregistered analysis, we hypothesized that correlations between predicted and self-reported BFI traits would decrease with less conversational text.
To test this, we had the rater generate predictions with 13 and 5 turns from each conversation.
Participants produced a median of 204 words (range: 56 to 784) in the 13 turn transcript, and 80 words (range: 18 to 476) in the 5 turn transcript.
Figure 2B shows how correlations between the predicted scores and participants' self-reported scores for each BFI trait changed as the amount of conversation decreased.

text.text: With less than half the text of the original interaction, we observed significant positive correlations between predicted and self-reported BFI traits for four of the five traits (Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Extraversion, and Openness).
Correlations averaged r = .31 (range: .19 to .40).
With 5 turns, the rater predicted only two of the five traits (Neuroticism and Openness) better than chance, and the average correlation was r = .20 (range: .09 to .29; see Appendix 2).
Across traits, we used one-way repeated measures ANOVA to compare how MSE between predicted and self-reported trait scores changed as the amount of conversation changed.
Compared to 26 conversational turns, MSE increased as the number of turns decreased (F(1.56, 152.86) = 31.82, p < .001, ηp² = .25).

text.text: Thus, the rater's ability to predict BFI traits depended on the amount of conversation, although the rater could predict some traits like Neuroticism with as few as 5 conversational turns.
A lexical hypothesis of personality proposes that personality traits are represented in language (Allport & Odbert, 1936; Galton, 1884; Goldberg, 1993).

text.text: This suggests that the rater's trait predictions might be driven by word choice, with little contribution from conversational context (what the AI said) and syntax.

To test this, we assessed the rater's ability to predict participants' BFI traits following the removal of 1) the AI's responses and 2) all filler words and temporal context, providing the rater with only a categorized list of the nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that participants wrote, alphabetized within each syntactic category.
Figure 2C shows this data.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">2C</ref> shows this data.

text.text: Excluding the AI's messages had little impact on the correlation between LLM predicted and self-reported BFI traits.
All five correlations were significant, averaging r = .36 (range: .20 to .47).

When the LLM's predictions were based solely on the content words participants produced, only Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism were predicted at better than chance, and the average correlation fell to r = .27 (range: .19 to .34; see Appendix 2).
Across traits, we used one-way repeated measures ANOVA to compare how MSE between predicted and self-reported trait scores changed as the type of information used in the prediction changed.

Providing the rater with the full participant-AI conversation versus what participants wrote versus only the content words and pronouns participants wrote did not reliably change the rater's prediction (F(1.45, 141.85) = 2.16, p = .134, ηp² = .02).
Figure 2D (bottom panel) depicts these results as the change in MSE as the type of information was changed (see Appendix 2).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">2D</ref> (bottom panel) depicts these results as the change in MSE as the type of information was changed (see Appendix 2).

text.text: With the correlational analyses, this suggests that the words participants used in conversation, as opposed to how they combined them, were the best signals of personality.
Experiment 1 demonstrated that meaningful personality signals can be detected in short, unstructured interactions with AI.
In Experiment 2, we tested the extent to which the AI's instructed personality might influence these signals.
Using a similar method to Experiment 1, 95 participants completed the BFI, and then had an unstructured chat with two LLMs.

One LLM was prompted to mimic participants' self-reported personality traits in language and conversation style, while the other was prompted to mimic the opposite of participants' personality traits.
Participants wrote a median of 377 words (range: 131 to 1007) when they spoke with the mirror AI, and 394 words (range: 142 to 1056) when they spoke with the inverse AI.
There was no difference in the number of words they produced with each (t(94) = -1.31, p = .19, dz = -.13).
Like Experiment 1, the rater was given the transcript from each interaction and instructed to identify elements in the text that revealed information about the participant's personality.
The rater then completed the BFI acting like each participant, and we compared these scores with self-report.
Figure 3A shows correlations between rater-predicted trait scores and participants' self-reported trait scores.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref> shows correlations between rater-predicted trait scores and participants' self-reported trait scores.

text.text: When predictions were based on transcripts of conversations with the mirror AI, correlations with self-reported traits averaged r = .41, with four of five traits predicted better than chance (see Appendix 2).
As in Experiment 1, the highest correlation was observed for Neuroticism (r(93) = .63, 95% CI [.49, .74], p < .001) and the lowest for Conscientiousness (r(93) = .14, 95% CI [-.06, .33], p = .17).

text.text: When predictions were based on conversations with the inverse AI, correlations averaged r = .30 (range: .15 to .44), with only three of five traits predicted better than chance.

The rater's ability to predict Neuroticism was significantly better when the prediction was based on conversations with the LLM that mirrored participants' personality (r = .63 vs r = .18: t(92) = 6.50, p < .001).

text.text: Importantly, this pattern of results was similar when the rater's predictions were based only on the messages participants sent, rather than on the entire conversation (see Appendix 2).
Next, we compared differences in MSE from self-report between predictions based on conversations with the mirror AI, and predictions based on conversations with the inverse AI.
There was an interaction between LLM personality (mirror versus inverse) and error associated with each trait (F(3.20, 300.8) = 7.84, p < .001, ηp² = .08).

text.text: The rater predicted Neuroticism with more error when the prediction was based on chats with the inverse AI compared to the mirror AI (t(94) = 4.86, p < .001, dz = .50).

text.text: As in Experiment 1 (Figure 2C), we examined the extent to which the rater's prediction was based on the words participants chose to use as opposed to conversational context and syntax.

text.text: Participants produced a median of 243 (range: 87 to 684) content words and pronouns with the mirror AI, and 262 (range: 97 to 720) content words and pronouns with the inverse AI.
There was no difference in the number of these words participants wrote with each (t(94) = -1.15, p = .25, dz = -.12).

Figure 3C shows correlations between the rater's predicted BFI trait scores and participants' self-reported scores when the rater's prediction was based solely on the content words and pronouns participants wrote.

text.text: For words shared with the mirror AI, these correlations averaged r = .40 (range: .21 to .60) and all five traits were predicted better than chance.
None of the correlations were significant when they were based on words shared with the inverse AI (average r = .03, range: -.25 to .15).

For three of five traits, we observed a statistical difference between predictions using words shared with the mirror AI and those shared with the inverse AI-Neuroticism (r = .60 vs r = -.25: t(92) = 8.49, p < .001), Extraversion (r = .44 vs r = .04: t(92) = 3.78, p < .01), and Openness (r = .45 vs r = .15: t(92) = 2.96, p < .05).

text.text: Finally, we explored whether the differences in Experiment 2 might reflect mimicry of the AI's language, rather than participants' own word choice.
To test this, we applied a conservative filter, removing content words produced by participants that were repetitions of lemmas (dictionary headwords) written by the AI in previous messages.
For example, if the AI used the words go and run, all variants used by the participant in later messages (e.g., running, ran, went, gone) were removed.
We then had the rater predict participants' traits based on the content words and pronouns that remained.
Although this strict approach likely removed words that genuinely reflected self-expression, it also controlled for mimicry.

Applying this filter left a median of 180 participant words (range: 65 to 540) with the mirror AI and 197 participant words (range: 54 to 543) with the inverse AI, with no statistical difference in word counts between these conditions (t(94) = -1.51, p = .14, dz = -.16).

Even with this restricted text, the rater predicted three of five traits in the case of words written to the mirror AI (Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion), and no traits in the case of the inverse AI.
A statistical difference was still observed for predictions of Neuroticism between the mirror and inverse conditions (r = .49 vs r = -.07: t(92) = 5.26, p < .001).

text.text: More generally, the pattern of correlations and MSE between rater-predicted and self-reported traits looked similar to that observed with all content words included (see Figure S1 and Tables S1-2).

text.text: Thus, the extent to which participants conveyed some traits solely through words they had not seen the AI produce depended on whether the AI's persona mirrored their personality.
We tested the extent to which unconstrained, text-based conversations with AI convey personality traits.
Participants had conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.
A second LLM then predicted participants' Big Five personality traits based on the text of the conversations.
Correlations with self-reported traits were positive and significant in each case.
As hypothesized, the rater's ability to predict personality decreased as the amount of conversation it had access to decreased.
But even with only half the conversation, four out of five personality traits were predicted at better than chance.
A linguistic analysis revealed that in conversations with AI people conveyed their personality through word choice, with syntax and conversational context playing a smaller role.
In a second study, we applied Experiment 1's method to data involving conversations with AI that either mirrored or opposed participants' personalities.
In this case, linguistic signals of personality were especially strong in conversations when the AI's persona mirrored participants' personalities.

Unlike traits such as height and eye colour, personality isn't a static property of people-it's primarily measured using self-report and these measurements reflect the social and psychological context in which they occurred.

In reflection of this, the test-retest reliability of personality questionnaires like the BFI or other inventories ranges from .7 to .8 (Gnambs, 2014; John & Srivastava, 1999; McCrae et al., 2011)-lower than other psychological traits such as IQ (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/vXoX. Brown & May, 1979).

text.text: How meaningful is a personality prediction that correlates with self-report at r = .37?
Comparisons with similar personality predictions made by friends and family help contextualize the predictions observed here.

Using meta-analysis, Connelly and Ones (2010) report that, across traits, predictions of personality made by friends (defined as people with a mutual liking who have known each other for a median of 3 years) correlate with self-report at .35.
text.formatted: Using meta-analysis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Connelly and Ones (2010)</ref> report that, across traits, predictions of personality made by friends (defined as people with a mutual liking who have known each other for a median of 3 years) correlate with self-report at .35.

text.text: In the case of family (defined as people linked by genetics or marriage who have known each other for a median of 17 years) the same correlation was .43.
The predictions generated here from short conversations with AI align with these values, and, for some traits, numerically exceed them.
Thus, the predictions were meaningful in the sense that they were as good as predictions made by people who know each other well, in some cases, extraordinarily so (e.g., spouses and family members).

In Experiment 1, predictions of personality from conversations with AI were similar between predictions made using the full conversations and predictions that relied solely on the content words and pronouns that participants shared.
This was also observed in Experiment 2, but only when the AI's personality mirrored participants' personality.
When the AI's personality opposed participants' personality, three significant trait predictions collapsed when only the participants' content words and pronouns were considered.
In this case, syntax may have helped the rater avoid confusing displays of empathy with words that signaled personality.

The words in the sentence, I'm sorry you're feeling depressed, for example, could be confused as a signal of depression when viewed as an alphabetized list of content words and pronouns (Pham et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The words in the sentence, I'm sorry you're feeling depressed, for example, could be confused as a signal of depression when viewed as an alphabetized list of content words and pronouns <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Pham et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, how people combine words can convey meaningful signals of personality in some circumstances.
People readily convey personality in short conversations with AI, but they don't convey all traits equally.
Here, Neuroticism was the strongest signal.
In Experiment 1, the correlation between predictions of this trait and self-report was .47; in Experiment 2, when the AI's prompted personality mirrored participants, it was .63.
This is potentially problematic.

Neuroticism is associated with anxiety and depression (Kotov et al.https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/ophN+HC3B 2010; Malouff et al., 2005) , and, as noted, LLMs converge their output towards the word choice and linguistic style of conversational partners (Blevins, 2026; P. Chen et al., 2026).

text.text: Future work should test the extent to which LLM mimicry of Neuroticism might exacerbate disorders of mental health.
Critically, Experiment 2 also demonstrated that when the AI exhibited an opposite personality to participants, linguistic signatures of Neuroticism collapsed.
One safeguard against the reinforcement of negative psychological traits by AI might be through the regulation of the personas AI are instructed to mimic.
What role do LLMs play in psychological measurement?

There's a longstanding tension in psychology between self-report measures of psychological variables and more implicit measurements from computer-based tasks (Corneille & Gawronski, 2024; Moreau, 2025; Zimmerman, 2024).
text.formatted: There's a longstanding tension in psychology between self-report measures of psychological variables and more implicit measurements from computer-based tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Corneille & Gawronski, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Moreau, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Zimmerman, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Computerized behavioural tasks quantify psychological traits by fitting formal computational models developed from neurocognitive theory to raw behavioural data (Corlett & Fletcher, 2014; Montague et al., 2012; Wilson & Collins, 2019)-a tradition echoing behaviourism's rejection of introspection (Watson, 1913).

text.text: Psychometricians counter that implicit measures lack crucial properties of validated self-report questionnaires, like test-retest reliability, efficiency of administration, and predictive validity for real-world outcomes (Corneille & Gawronski, 2024).

text.text: LLMs offer a method to bridge self-report with more implicit measures of psychology (Wright et al., 2026).

text.text: Conversation is one of the most common human behaviours.

By applying psychometric principles to the text of raw, unconstrained conversations-which can be less susceptible to the social desirability biases that shape self-report (Paulhus, 1984; Vazire, 2010)-LLMs can reproduce self-report psychometric scores directly from natural language.

text.text: For example, Suthaharan et al. (2026) used an LLM to rate metacognition from free-text descriptions after a behavioural task, and LLM-inferred metacognition moderated task performance.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Suthaharan et al. (2026)</ref> used an LLM to rate metacognition from free-text descriptions after a behavioural task, and LLM-inferred metacognition moderated task performance.

text.text: In combination with the current study and related work, this provides evidence that LLMs can be used to combine the psychometric rigour of self-report with the naturalism of human behaviour.

Although our findings demonstrate that an LLM can infer personality traits from the language people chose to share in conversations with AI, the extent to which AI can glean personality from human-to-human conversations is unclear.
When people are asked to rate the personality of others following short interactions, their predictions weakly correlate with self-report (Wall et al., 2013).
text.formatted: When people are asked to rate the personality of others following short interactions, their predictions weakly correlate with self-report <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Wall et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: People may reveal more about their personality traits in conversations with AI, as these conversations might feel less observed and AI systems are good at mimicking empathy.

For example, Lucas et al., (2014) demonstrated that participants were willing to disclose more personal information to a virtual human when they believed it was being controlled by a computer versus a person.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Lucas et al., (2014)</ref> demonstrated that participants were willing to disclose more personal information to a virtual human when they believed it was being controlled by a computer versus a person.

text.text: Third party raters perceived AI responses as more compassionate than human responses, even when they knew the response was AI-generated (Ovsyannikova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Third party raters perceived AI responses as more compassionate than human responses, even when they knew the response was AI-generated <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Ovsyannikova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: But other evidence is more mixed. Croes et al. (2024) found no difference in participants' self-rated intimacy of disclosures between disclosures to chatbots and humans, but there was less fear of judgement when disclosing to a chatbot.
text.formatted: But other evidence is more mixed. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Croes et al. (2024)</ref> found no difference in participants' self-rated intimacy of disclosures between disclosures to chatbots and humans, but there was less fear of judgement when disclosing to a chatbot.

text.text: The extent to which people share their psychology through word choice with LLMs versus other people has yet to be directly tested.
This paper presents a framework for pursuing this work.
In a preregistered study, we demonstrated that human personality is expressed through short, unstructured interactions with AI.
Participants conveyed personality largely through word choice, and this was especially true when the LLM's personality mirrored participants.
These personality signals were meaningful, matching self-other predictions from friends and, in some cases, family.
Some traits like Neuroticism could be identified with only a few hundred words of conversation.
Thus, signals of personality are recoverable from short, unstructured conversations with AI.
Given the extent to which humans now engage with LLMs, people may be sharing more about their psychology with AI systems than they realize.

text.text: For example: Extraversion: use sociable, enthusiastic, and energetic language if high; use reserved, quiet, and reflective language if low.
Conscientiousness: Use organized, precise, and responsible language if high; use easy-going, spontaneous, or sometimes careless language if low.
Openness: Use imaginative, creative, and curious language if high; use conventional, practical, and traditional language if low.
Agreeableness: Use warm, friendly, and cooperative language if high; use skeptical, critical, or blunt language if low.
Neuroticism: Use anxious, sensitive, or self-conscious language if high; use calm, steady, and emotionally stable language if low.
Do not state your BFI scores explicitly or describe your personality directly-let it show naturally through your language.
In addition, you are a person chatting casually with a new friend (never reveal you are an AI).
Use a mix of statements, reflections, and the occasional question, as people do in real conversations when they're getting to know each other.
Keep your responses to 2 or 3 sentences.
